headline: Global crude exports reach record despite Strait of Hormuz disruption
body:
What happened: Global crude oil exports reached a record high even though the Strait of Hormuz was closed, according to the reporting. Shipments from producers in the Gulf were disrupted by the closure, yet other suppliers and rerouted flows kept total volumes at a peak. Buyers across Asia and Europe have been the main recipients of the redirected supply.

The development matters for importers that depend on Gulf crude, including large economies in Asia, and for oil prices, which tend to react to chokepoint disruptions. Malaysia, a regional oil and gas exporter, is also watching the trend closely as it tracks its own record export performance.

Reported by: Nikkei Asia. Also covered by Bloomberg, Focus Taiwan, Taipei Times.

headline: Bitcoin slides under $60,000 as AI valuation fears hit risk assets
body:
What happened: Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency, dropped below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since July, trading near $59,381 after a 3.45 per cent fall. Ether, the second-largest digital coin, fell about 5.23 per cent to roughly $1,649. Traders pointed to worries about whether heavy spending on AI infrastructure will pay off, higher borrowing costs, and regulatory uncertainty after Democrats won the US midterm elections, along with the departure of Nvidia's chief executive. Major US stock indexes were also set for their steepest weekly fall since April 2025.

Reported by: CNA. Also covered by Reuters, Yahoo Finance.

headline: Anthropic shares jump in Nasdaq debut, valuing AI firm near $2 trillion
body:
What happened: Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, debuted on the Nasdaq on November 20, with shares opening 34 per cent above the $83 offer price and its market value briefly reaching $2 trillion. The company sold 980 million shares, priced above its initial range, and its proceeds could rise to about $93.5 billion if underwriters exercise their extra share option. Investors welcomed the listing as a test of appetite for AI companies, following Nvidia's earnings report earlier in the week. Analysts cautioned that demand may reflect fear of missing out, and questioned profitability given large computing commitments.

Reported by: Business Insider. Also covered by Reuters, MarketWatch, Daily Sabah, Yahoo Finance.

headline: US extends AI chip export curbs to remote access by Chinese firms
body:
What happened: Washington has widened its export controls on advanced AI chips so they now cover remote access, not only physical shipments. Under the change, data centers that rent out computing power, including operators in Southeast Asia and Brazil, come under licensing scrutiny, narrowing a route that Chinese AI developers had used to reach the hardware. The move follows a scandal involving Nvidia chips and reports in the articles describe chip-sector stocks sliding in China, Taiwan and South Korea. Analysts' views on the full effect were not settled in the reporting.

Reported by: Fortune. Also covered by Bloomberg, Financial Times, Al Jazeera, CNA.

headline: EU budget chair floats fresh cuts and a digital tax for 2028-2034
body:
What happened: The European Union's leaders' chair has put forward a revised draft of the bloc's 2028-2034 long-term budget, proposing further spending cuts to bridge a divide among member states. The draft also floats a tax on large technology firms as a possible new source of EU revenue. Reports cite a figure of around €200 billion in reductions, though the final shape of the package remains open to negotiation among member governments.

The proposal affects EU member states that are net contributors to the budget and those expecting larger shares of funding, as well as major digital companies that could face the new levy. Markets have not been reported as moving sharply, but the outcome will shape long-term EU spending priorities and national budget planning.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Bloomberg, Barron's.

headline: Alphabet plans C$6 billion bond sale in Canada to fund AI spending
body:
What happened: Alphabet, Google's parent company, plans to raise C$6 billion, roughly $4.19 billion, through several tranches of unsecured notes sold in the Canadian market, according to pricing terms it released. The offering reflects a broader shift among large technology firms, which are increasingly turning to debt and equity markets to finance AI infrastructure rather than relying only on cash. Alphabet said the proceeds would go toward general corporate purposes, which could include repaying existing debt. RBC Dominion Securities, Scotia Capital and TD Securities are joint lead managers, with CIBC World Markets as co-manager.

Reported by: Yahoo Finance. Also covered by Reuters, Financial Times, The Globe and Mail, CNA.

headline: Anthropic's stock slips as AI selloff hits Wall Street and global markets
body:
What happened: Anthropic shares debuted on the Nasdaq after a record IPO priced at $83, opening well above that level and closing about 17 per cent higher on the first day. The gains faded in after-hours trading as a broad selloff in AI stocks pulled the new listing below $92. Wall Street's S&P 500 fell 2 per cent overnight, weighed by AI jitters, rate fears and trade tensions.

The drop spread to Australia, where the ASX 200 fell 1.6 per cent to 8592.6 and posted its worst week since June 2020, with technology and mining stocks leading losses. Analysts including Melius Research and Needham had launched coverage with bullish ratings before the debut, with price targets well above the IPO price.

Reported by: Bloomberg. Also covered by Reuters, AP, Financial Times, The Wall Street Journal.

headline: Japan Tobacco expects large loss after Russian units are taken under state control
body:
What happened: Japan Tobacco said it will record a loss of about 1.38 trillion yen, roughly $8.7 billion, after it lost control of its Russian subsidiaries when President Vladimir Putin ordered their seizure. The company, about 37 per cent owned by the Japanese government, now forecasts a net loss of 724 billion yen for the year to December 31, reversing an earlier profit outlook. It also cut its annual dividend forecast to 204 yen from 234 yen. Shares have fallen roughly 25 per cent since the decree.

Russia had contributed about a quarter of group profits, and those units will now be excluded from consolidated earnings. Chief executive Takehiko Tsutsui said the company will keep investing in growth, with operations outside Russia expected to lift operating profit by more than 10 per cent from 2027 to 2029.

Reported by: AP. Also covered by Bloomberg, The New York Times, MarketWatch, Barron's.

headline: IMF study finds fiscal macroframeworks help make stabilizing policy credible
body:
What happened: The International Monetary Fund has published a working paper on how countries' macroeconomic frameworks affect whether fiscal policy can stabilize the economy. The study examines whether a credible framework, such as a clear fiscal rule or medium-term plan, lets governments use budget measures to offset downturns and booms without losing investors' trust. The paper draws on the IMF's own research methods and cross-country fiscal data; specific country samples and time periods should be checked in the full text.

The findings matter for finance ministries, central banks and bond markets, since credibility shapes borrowing costs. Analysts would view the results as relevant to how governments design budget rules in advanced and emerging economies alike.

Reported by: IMF.

headline: California probes Nvidia over possible chip diversion to China and investor disclosures
body:
What happened: California's attorney general, Rob Bonta, has issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia, the US chip designer, after the departure of its longtime chief executive, Jensen Huang. Bonta said the state is examining whether Nvidia or Huang's conduct allowed China to obtain advanced chips or confidential information, and whether the company misled investors. Nvidia has been contacted for comment. Separately, reports link Huang to a suspected Chinese spy at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre firm and major Nvidia customer, which Congress members want the US Commerce Department to examine.

Nvidia's shares have fallen about 22% since early November, when the affair was first reported. Chinese AI firms and the broader US-China technology trade are watching closely, as any finding of chip diversion could tighten export controls affecting China's access to American hardware.

Reported by: AP. Also covered by Bloomberg, Financial Times, The Wall Street Journal, BBC News.

Democratic lawmakers back the export controls but want broader regulation of the AI industry, while China calls the measures economic coercion. Analysts doubt the rule will significantly slow China's chip ambitions, and Washington may struggle to enforce it.

headline: World Bank study measures the economic cost of power outages in developing economies
body:
What happened: A World Bank study examines how frequent electricity outages, and the diesel generators businesses use to cope with them, weigh on developing economies. The report draws on the bank's enterprise survey data gathered from firms across many low and middle income countries, and it links outage frequency to lost output, higher operating costs and reduced productivity.

The findings point to firms in developing economies paying a sizeable hidden cost for unreliable grids, since generator fuel and maintenance cut into margins and reduce investment. The analysis suggests that reliable power is a precondition for growth in these markets.

Reported by: World Bank.

headline: US judge approves $7.25 billion Bayer settlement over Roundup cancer claims
body:
What happened: A Missouri state judge in St Louis has approved Bayer's $7.25 billion settlement of lawsuits alleging its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer. The judge called the deal fair and rejected objections that individual payouts were too low, warning that delays could leave terminally ill claimants waiting years. Bayer had faced about 65,000 claims, and its share price has fallen 46% since it bought Monsanto in 2018. The approval follows a US Supreme Court ruling that federal pesticide law bars certain state failure-to-warn claims, and about 200 federal cases remain outside the settlement.

Reported by: AP. Also covered by Bloomberg, Financial Times, The Guardian, The New York Times.

headline: Trump says Canada trade talks need more work before a fair deal
body:
What happened: US President Donald Trump said more work remains before a fair trade agreement with Canada can be reached, and suggested Canada had grown bold in its position. Separately, reports indicate Ottawa is pushing for a smaller interim arrangement with Washington that could bring relief from US tariffs, possibly before the end of the year. Sources say Canadian officials have seen little movement from the American side on easing those tariffs so far. A US senator has urged Canada to accept an interim tariff agreement while Congress takes up a longer-term deal.

For Canada, the stakes are high: its exporters, especially in autos, steel and lumber, depend heavily on the US market, and tariff relief would lower their costs. Markets have watched the talks closely, since any interim deal would shape cross-border trade flows and business planning on both sides of the border.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by CBC News, BNN Bloomberg.

headline: Trump vows penalties for US firms building AI data centers overseas
body:
What happened: President Donald Trump said on Friday that American companies building data centers abroad would face a "tremendous tax," arguing the move would help the US artificial intelligence sector compete with China. He did not explain how the penalty would work or what legal authority would support it. Data centers are central to the AI boom, and developers often place them near users to cut delays and data transmission costs, so a penalty could complicate the global buildout. Separately, US export controls on advanced AI chips have tightened, affecting data center operators in Southeast Asia.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by AP, Bloomberg, Financial Times, BBC News.

headline: SpaceX secures $44 billion debt for Nvidia AI chip purchases
body:
What happened: Apollo and Goldman Sachs have priced roughly $44 billion of debt to fund SpaceX's purchase of Nvidia GPU chips and related equipment. The firms describe it as the largest AI-related chip financing arranged to date, and demand from investors was strong enough to let the deal be upsized. The money is expected to support SpaceX's rollout of Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips as it expands its AI computing capacity.

The largest tranche, $25.17 billion of senior secured notes due 2033, priced at a yield of 8.259 per cent. Lease payments are set to begin when the equipment is delivered in the first half of 2027. The deal highlights how heavily AI expansion relies on borrowing, with BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and KKR-advised accounts providing anchor commitments.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Financial Times, CNA.

headline: US presses Singapore and Malaysia to tighten checks on Iranian oil trade
body:
What happened: The United States Treasury has urged Singapore and Malaysia to do more to make sure their financial and shipping sectors comply with American sanctions on Iran. The push targets trade and transactions that could help move Iranian oil and other sanctioned goods through the two Southeast Asian hubs. Banks, traders and shipping firms in both countries could face closer scrutiny and higher compliance costs as a result. Details of specific enforcement steps were not confirmed in the reporting available.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Arab News, The Jakarta Post.

headline: Societe Generale forecasts S&P 500 at 8,500 by end-2027
body:
What happened: Societe Generale, the French bank, has projected that the S&P 500 index of major US stocks will close 2027 at 8,500 points. The forecast rests on expected gains from artificial intelligence and on continued strength in corporate earnings. Only headlines were available for the related coverage, so no further detail on the bank's assumptions could be confirmed. Investors in US equities, including funds and pension holders worldwide, would be affected if the call proves accurate. Separate coverage of Goldman Sachs points to inflation easing by the end of 2027, which could shape the rate outlook for US stocks.

headline: Dollar slips from multi-month high as AI worries and Fed bets shift
body:
What happened: The US dollar eased on Friday, ending a rally of about eight sessions as it lost momentum after hitting its highest level since April 2025. The dollar index dropped 0.2 per cent to 103.75, though it remained up 1.7 per cent for the month. The rally had been driven by hotter-than-expected US inflation data and expectations that the Federal Reserve would stay hawkish, including a suggestion from Fed Governor Christopher Waller of a possible December rate hike.

Lower US Treasury yields, pushed down by AI-related worries that weighed on global stocks, helped lift lower-yielding currencies such as the Swiss franc and the yen. Japan's core inflation rose to 2.2 per cent in October, strengthening expectations of a Bank of Japan rate hike. Sterling stayed near a one-year low against the dollar, and bitcoin fell to a four-month low.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Bloomberg, Financial Times, CNA.

headline: Could the Fed consider a surprise rate hike amid current economic conditions?
body:
What happened: Federal Reserve officials are reportedly weighing whether a larger-than-usual interest rate increase could be warranted, with at least one policymaker publicly floating a half-point move. Commentators questioned whether such a hike fits the present economic backdrop, and some suggested investors should reposition their holdings in case rates climb further. Markets have already moved: currencies across Latin America fell as traders priced in tighter US policy. Banks such as JPMorgan may gain from higher rates, though analysts note the trade-off is not clear-cut. Market-implied odds of a hike were described as very high, though these estimates may shift.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Bloomberg, Barron's, Yahoo Finance.

headline: Anthropic lists on Nasdaq in record IPO, but markets close lower
body:
What happened: AI developer Anthropic, maker of the Claude assistant, began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, in the largest initial public offering on record. The company raised its offer size and price, selling 980 million shares at $83 each, and the stock opened about 34 percent higher before closing at $97.17. Broader US indexes fell sharply, with the Nasdaq down 2.2 percent, as investors took profits and tech shares such as Nvidia and AMD dropped. Investors in the United States and Nvidia, Amazon and Google, which have large ties to Anthropic, are closely watching the stock.

Reported by: Financial Times. Also covered by Bloomberg, The Wall Street Journal, Al Jazeera, France 24.

headline: Economists warn Australia may be sliding toward recession as retail and sanctions news emerge
body:
What happened: Economists have warned that Australia is showing signs typical of a recession, a development that bears on households and businesses across the country. Separately, David Jones plans to cut about 1,500 jobs, roughly a quarter of its workforce, while shutting 19 of its 38 stores as the debt-laden department store fights for survival. Australia has also imposed sanctions on three Israeli individuals and four organisations over illegal settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, a narrower step than the wider trade ban adopted by the UK and other European allies.

Reported by: Bloomberg. Also covered by The Wall Street Journal, BBC News, DW, Barron's.
